entries.knownHazards: The seeds probably contain hydrogen cyanide. This is the ingredient that gives almonds their characteristic flavour. Unless the seed is very bitter it should be perfectly safe in reasonable quantities. In small quantities, hydrogen cyanide has been shown to stimulate respiration and improve digestion, it is also claimed to be of benefit in the treatment of cancer. In excess, however, it can cause respiratory failure and even death.

entries.knownHazards: No reports of toxicity have been seen for this species, but the following reports have been seen for S. officinale. This plant contains small quantities of a toxic alkaloid which can have a cumulative effect upon the liver. Largest concentrations are found in the roots, leaves contain higher quantities of the alkaloid as they grow older and young leaves contain almost none. Most people would have to consume very large quantities of the plant in order to do any harm, though anyone with liver problems should obviously be more cautious. In general, the health-promoting properties of the plant probably far outweigh any possible disbenefits, especially if only the younger leaves are used.

entries.knownHazardsLtFinal: Tiesioginio toksiškumo duomenų šiai rūšiai nėra, tačiau giminingoje S. officinale aptiktas toksiškas alkaloidas, galintis kauptis kepenyse — didžiausios jo koncentracijos šaknyse ir senuose lapuose. Esant kepenų ligoms, reikia atsargumo; jauniausi lapai saugiausi.

The LT (both V2 and Edited) omits this critical caveat and presents the hazard as applying directly to this species, which misrepresents the EN source. The uncertainty/cross-species disclaimer must be included.

entries.knownHazards: Although we have found no reports of toxicity for this species, a number of ferns contain carcinogens so some caution is advisable[200]. Many ferns also contain thiaminase, an enzyme that robs the body of its vitamin B complex. In small quantities this enzyme will do no harm to people eating an adequate diet that is rich in vitamin B, though large quantities can cause severe health problems. The enzyme is destroyed by heat or thorough drying, so cooking the plant will remove the thiaminase[172].

entries.flagReason: COMPOUND NAME: EN source lists 'thespesone' as a distinct compound. LT renders it as 'tespespozonas' — the double 'sp' sequence ('tespes-ponas'→'tespespozonas') appears to be a typographic error introduced in V2 and carried through to Edited. The correct Lithuanianized form should be 'tespozonas' (thespone) and 'tespespozonas' is likely a garbled fusion of 'tesponas' and 'tespespozonas'. EN has four compounds: mansonone D, mansonone H, thespone, thespesone — all four must be distinct in LT.
entries.suggestedFix: Correct the compound name list: 'mansononas D ir H, tesponas, tespezponas' or keep the EN names in parentheses for clarity: 'mansononas D ir H, tesponas ir tespesponas'. Review exact transliteration of 'thespesone' — likely 'tespespozanas' is incorrect; suggest 'tespesponas'.
